articles.title: The Uprising Wastes a Good Class-Struggle Story
articles.author: Jeremy Gong
articles.content: In 1381, more than a hundred thousand poor English people rose up demanding an end to serfdom. During the uprising, they killed a coterie of hated government officials, and, in turn, the fourteen-year-old King Richard II massacred thousands of them. The best-remembered figure of the English Peasants’ Revolt is one of its leaders, John Ball, whose speeches and sermons captured the spirit of what would eventually, centuries later, develop into socialism. “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?” he famously asked, meaning that in the Garden of Eden, the Bible’s first people labored only for their own sustenance, with no concepts of lords and serfs. As a socialist and fan of medieval period pieces, I was excited to see the new film The Uprising , which dramatizes the English Peasants’ Revolt and stars Andrew Garfield as a fed-up farmer-rebel. The subject matter has the makings of a thrilling class-struggle movie — and indeed, Garfield and director Paul Greengrass ( Captain Phillips , two films in the Bourne trilogy, and Bloody Sunday ) promoted the movie as a tale of resistance to oligarchy. As The Hollywood Reporter writes , “ The Uprising feels strikingly of the moment. Modern-day oligarchs wield outsized influence over elections and self-enriching policies. Working people, meanwhile, continue to struggle with the rising cost of living.” The film’s director and star express hope that The Uprising will be “galvanizing.” “We’ve had enough,” declared Greengrass. “I hope there’s some awakening,” Garfield told a live audience this month. “And I hope that if any billionaires watch it,” he continued, that “they’re scared shitless.” It’s a welcome sign that Hollywood wants to tell these kinds of stories. But far from giving hope that the masses of ordinary people can make social change, The Uprising condemns social movements as self-defeating, promotes a misguided faith in select elites, and ends with a nihilistic moral of individual revenge. Billionaires have nothing to fear from The Uprising . Medieval Class War The fourteenth century was a grim time for the common people of England. Kings threw thousands of lives away in a failed effort to take the French throne, known as the Hundred Years’ War, which bankrupted the state in the process. As much as half of England’s population died in the black plague in the mid 1300s. Many rural poor were serfs. Serfs had their own plots of land to feed themselves, but for that privilege they had to work on their lord’s land for free and pay exorbitant fees. Serfs and their children were bound to their land and their lord forever, not unlike slaves. Other peasants were free but still chafed at the high rents and violent control that their noble or ecclesiastical landlords exerted over them. Despite its modern designation as the Peasants’ Revolt, many of those who would rebel in 1381 were not landholding peasants but unlanded laborers and artisans who worked for a wage — the proto-working class. A common source of rage for peasants and workers alike was that their employers were also their landlords, lawmakers, judges, and jailers. As Marxist historian Rodney Hilton writes in Bond Men Made Free , the rebellion would be “one of the whole people below the ranks of those who exercised lordship.” By the late 1300s, these groups had begun pushing for political rights, lower rents, and higher wages. The plague, while traumatic, increased their leverage: labor demand now far exceeded supply, and depopulated land needed tenants. Thus, peasants and workers benefited from greater bargaining power vis-à-vis their superiors, and they pressed their demands with protests, petitions, and riots. This plebeian agitation threatened the social system and outraged England’s rulers. In response, they passed a series of laws to keep the poor in their place. One law fixed wages at their pre-plague, pre-inflation rates. Another commanded that those who abandoned their employer to seek better pay be branded on the forehead with an F for “falsity.” This ongoing class struggle forms the backdrop for The Uprising ’s opening scenes, where the king’s greedy, gold-encrusted advisers decide to once again tax the common people to pay for the crown’s losing war. The 1381 “poll tax,” a flat tax for every person over the age of fifteen, was the straw that broke the camel’s back. One particularly hated official even conceived of an invasive “puberty test” to check who was of age. The Great Unwashed The story of 1381 should encourage a healthy hatred of the rich and sympathy for the poor, and The Uprising gets off to a strong though lurid start. Tax collectors come to the village of the rustic Ploughman, a fictional farmer turned reluctant leader played by Garfield, and push people around. After the third teen girl is violated by a soldier’s puberty check, Ploughman’s rage at the medieval Epstein class boils over: “That’s enough!” he shouts, before cutting them down with his scythe. Ploughman soon meets the historical leaders of the movement, the outlaw preacher John Ball (Jamie Bell) and the soldier turned revolutionary Wat Tyler (Cosmo Jarvis). We get to see Ball deliver his famous line about Adam and Eve to a cheering crowd — but missing from the speech is Tyler and Ball’s more temporal vision for an egalitarian society. One chronicler reports Ball calling for a society in which “all things shall be held in common, when there shall be neither vassals nor lords, when the lords shall be no more masters than ourselves.” Unfortunately, The Uprising gives us little chance to appreciate the radical and modern vision animating the rebels. In fact, the movie — perhaps unwittingly — seems to hold the mass of commoners who comprise the movement in contempt. Besides the leaders of the movement and a fictional love interest for Ploughman (the fanatical Alyce played by Thomasin McKenzie, hair cropped close like Joan of Arc), the entire crowd of thousands is little more than background scenery. There’s hardly a close-up of even one rank-and-file rebel, and in the background their faces are usually blurred. This illustration shows the priest John Ball on a horse, encouraging Wat Tyler’s rebels of 1381, from a ca. 1470 manuscript of Jean Froissart’s Chronicles in the British Library. This is a far cry from the historical epics Greengrass claimed to be emulating like Gladiator or Braveheart , and further still from the plebeian-centric films of leftist directors like Ken Loach. In one incredible scene from Land and Freedom , Loach’s 1995 movie about the Spanish Civil War, peasants and antifascist militants debate whether they should redistribute their former lords’ land in the context of civil war, imperialism, and revolution. If Loach imbues the poor with full, vibrant, and dignified interiority, Greengrass mostly collapses them into a threatening swarm. In The Uprising , virtually no peasant besides the protagonist even speaks a line that isn’t a background shout or scream. Given the opportunity to exact revenge on their rulers, the mob goes completely wild. In an animalistic frenzy, they not only decapitate their foes but bask in their grisly victory with smiles and songs. Alyce is shown speaking in tongues during one lynching. At the height of their power, the mob invades the Tower of London, where they capture and behead several of the king’s hated advisers. The mob goes on to attack anyone who looks rich and even start scapegoating Flemish immigrants. Their leaders are soon overwhelmed by the bloodthirsty mob in a slow-motion montage of carnage reminiscent of the D-Day landing in Saving Private Ryan — except that, besides Ball, Tyler, and Ploughman, all the rabble are joyfully hacking away. The next morning, an ashamed Ball and Tyler try to make sense of the massacres. Ball, the most extreme of the revolutionary leaders, explains to Ploughman that “If the end be well then all be well.” The film further establishes a parallel between the rebel leaders and the king’s hated council. The base passions on both sides — pride and a lust for power, wealth, and revenge — hasten the tragic massacres. The mob, meanwhile, is easily manipulated, and Richard slaughters them before they can consolidate their victories. For all their talk of striking terror into the heart of billionaires, one senses that the film’s architects are consummate liberals. The Uprising’ s John Ball is certainly how liberals see the revolutionary misleaders of the twentieth century, whose lofty goals were betrayed by cynical ends-justify-means tactics. And the message conveyed by the film’s attitude to the mob is familiar after a decade of centrists’ warnings about “populism,” left or right: radicals and the untamed masses they unleash are as much a problem as the oligarchs they oppose. Woody Norman and Katherine Waterston star as King Richard II and the queen mother, Joan of Kent, in The Uprising . (Blumhouse Productions) Nowhere is the film’s tepid liberalism more evident than in the character of the king’s mother. Throughout the film, the widowed Joan of Kent (Katherine Waterston) is portrayed as reasonable, compassionate, and moral. She objects to the punitive policies of the king’s advisers and supports the commoners. Joan becomes the moral voice of the movie, consonant with but more articulate than Ploughman himself. When the two later meet in London and together decry the mob violence on the streets outside, Joan puts forward a thesis straight out of The West Wing : it is reason and words that uplift, she says, “not the mob. Without words, there is only chaos and fear.” Later, after her son massacres his peasant detractors, Joan frowns her disapproval. In reality, of course, a member of the royal family would have had a vested interest in maintaining the feudal system, the wealth and power of the monarchy, and the church and aristocracy who upheld these. The poll tax that sparked the rebellion was, after all, meant to fund the monarchy’s war to conquer France. But in the gauzy moral world of The Uprising , Joan is Ploughman’s most important ally: if only the two of them could get her son’s ear and use their words, all the violence and suffering could be avoided. The Mangionification of Robin Hood Until the rising fails, Ploughman counsels moderation. When the rebels finally bring their demands to the king, Tyler asks for the end of serfdom, and Ball demands the executions of the royal councilors. Ploughman, more modest and less bloodthirsty (for now), declares with a straight face: “There will be no peace until we are healed.” But the king betrays them, and neither freedom, justice, nor “healing” is forthcoming. Failed by the idiotic mob, unable to persuade the king through his benevolent mother, only one option remains for our hero: individual vigilante violence. The movie jumps one year ahead and we see Ploughman and his band, all sporting green hooded capes, jumping from the woods to ambush the king’s entourage. Ploughman has become Robin Hood! Greengrass has made it clear that he intended The Uprising to be a Robin Hood origin story, and US promoters marketed the film as the “Rise of Robin Hood.” While he admits he is departing from historical accuracy, Greengrass wanted the film to have a happy ending after the uprising gets crushed, and the Robin Hood turn is his solution. So Ploughman returns as Robin Hood, but not to steal from the rich and give to the poor — which is the core of the traditional Robin Hood story and, while not transformative, is at least useful. Instead, this is Robin Hood as a Luigi Mangione figure, terrorizing the rich as payback. After killing the last of the king’s hated advisers in a rote and bloody duel, Ploughman delivers a speech befitting Joaquin Phoenix’s Joker. While Ploughman won’t kill the king (because “there’ll always be another”), he announces that now “we rule ourselves” in the forest, with “no kings.” Ploughman then promises to haunt the king’s dreams for the rest of his days. A knowing look is shared between Ploughman and the king’s mother, who apparently approves of this violence, maybe because it’s carried out by Andrew Garfield rather than the faceless mob. The film fades to a long shot of the king’s residence in the evening. We hear screaming and know the king’s sleep is indeed haunted by Ploughman and by the guilty conscience of everything he’s done. This is the happy ending Greengrass invents after the end of the rising. The horrid, stupid mob and their dishonest leaders are gone. The queen mother has failed to persuade the king to dismantle feudalism. At least our hero can carry out gruesome assassinations and disturb elites’ mental peace. I went into The Uprising hoping for a good class-struggle flick. But I left the theater feeling that this movie, rather than inspiring an “awakening,” will be discouraging for all but would-be vigilante terrorists. But don’t scare the rich too much! Since the film disregards the agency of the poor masses it should be celebrating, we’re left hoping that rich people come to their senses and save the day. Satisfied that The Uprising contributes to this goal, Garfield explains that “billionaires [are] the ones that might be the most soul sick. They’re the ones that might need healing the most.” When the Rabble Won Lucky for us, the real history of the 1381 English Peasants’ Revolt is itself galvanizing. Groups rose up simultaneously in different parts of the country, and then more risings followed as word spread. Peasants and laborers, led by sympathetic lower clergy or literate town leaders, demanded, and in some cases temporarily won, reprieve from feudal strictures and confiscatory fees, as well as local autonomy for villages and towns. The rebels did kill, and some Flemish migrants were slaughtered. (Hilton speculates these were the victims either of their competitors, the London weavers’ guild, or their employees, English journeymen weavers.) On balance, however, the rebels’ destruction was relatively contained and focused for a medieval army of more than one hundred thousand. Top government officials, all ultrawealthy nobles or church leaders themselves, were prime targets, as were their palaces. The most common targets for burning, however, were the documents that recorded the feudal dues and services owed to lords by their subjects. After King Richard II tricked and killed rebel leaders — Tyler was stabbed in the back, Ball drawn and quartered — he unleashed a campaign of bloodshed and terror far larger than that inflicted by the poor against the rich. While estimates vary, the revolt claimed the lives of between ninety and two hundred people; in the three months that followed its defeat, the king killed between 1,500 and 7,000. Surely his guilt-wracked mother frowned for each one. This is certainly depressing, but fortunately it is not, as Greengrass thinks, the end of the story. The revolt was crushed in 1381, but many of the demands of the movement were achieved over the coming years. The flat poll tax that incited the risings was abandoned, de facto and then de jure, as were the laws depressing wages. Some historians contend that serfdom was on its way out by this point anyway due to economic factors. However, it’s hard to believe that such a massive and well-organized show of popular power didn’t also discourage elites from enforcing their rights over their bondmen. As Robert Brenner writes : The revolt of 1381, despite the defeat of the peasant rising, seems to have opened the floodgates. Peasants now streamed away from their manors, and their lords could do nothing to stop them . . . By the second quarter of the fifteenth century, the vast majority of English peasants had won their freedom, and, as a consequence of their much improved bargaining position, were paying, at least for the time being, much lower rents. Through The Uprising , Greengrass and Garfield would warn us to keep aloof from the crowds and put our faith in a few enlightened elites who will right the ship. Failing that, we haunt their dreams. We have yet to see something so spectacular in the twenty-first century as the 1381 English Peasants’ Revolt, or even the labor and civil rights movements of the twentieth century, which also won enormous improvements in social welfare and individual liberty. The powers arrayed against us are enormous, and the conditions not always favorable. But while ordinary people do not choose our conditions, we can, as Karl Marx writes, make our own history. Fourteenth-century peasants couldn’t know that the society they won would become capitalism — more prosperous and free than feudalism but still unequal, chaotic, and violent. As the nineteenth-century socialist William Morris ponders in A Dream of John Ball , “Men fight and lose the battle, and the thing that they fought for comes about in spite of their defeat, and when it comes turns out not to be what they meant, and other men have to fight for what they meant under another name.” Today we’re carrying on the fight for John Ball’s radically egalitarian society. We owe a great deal to our forebears. The least we could do is give them a good class-struggle movie treatment, not The Uprising ’s nihilistic liberalism.

articles.title: The Prospects for a 2028 May Day Mass Strike
articles.author: Luis Feliz Leon
articles.content: Three years ago, the United Auto Workers (UAW), glowing with confidence after a successful strike at the Big Three and pledging ambitious new organizing drives, put out a call for a national strike on May 1, 2028. UAW President Shawn Fain called for unions to align their contracts with the Big Three to build leverage and create a crisis for the billionaire class. It was a new day in the UAW, and a wider labor renewal felt possible. May 2028 is now only a year and a half away. Are unions getting in gear for a season of strikes and labor action around then, as contracts expire in manufacturing, education, logistics, grocery, and the building trades? Some are. Labor Notes has found 830,000 workers with contracts planned or expected to expire from March to July 2028 (see illustration below). These include 150,000 autoworkers at the Big Three; 153,000 members of the American Postal Workers Union (APWU), though they are unlikely to strike; 95,000 grocery workers with the United Food and Commercial Workers Union (UFCW), and 77,000 K-12 educators with the California Teachers Association. “Together, we can turn May Day into a national day of reckoning,” Fain wrote last year, taking stock of the progress towards this goal. “If more union workers stand up together, we will all have more power to win what we’re owed.” Fighting on New Terrain What we are owed has been growing, amid Trump’s extreme attacks on workers and unions. One million federal workers have lost their right to collective bargaining. The National Labor Relations Board and other federal agencies meant to protect workers have been left unable to fulfill their essential roles. Tens of thousands of immigrant workers, including union members, have been stripped of their legal status and rights, subjected to criminalization and detention . Union contract expirations set for 2028. (Labor Notes) May Day 2028 wasn’t initially about fighting Trump’s billionaire power grab. But since Trump took office, the terrain has shifted. Mass protests have become more frequent and more urgently needed to stem the volley of attacks on workers and on democratic elections. Massive weekend protests that drew millions, organized by Indivisible and No Kings, haven’t been able to reverse Trump’s attacks, though they are important training grounds to welcome new activists. (Bring your union banner !) The next big one, “ No Kings: Vote Early ,” is scheduled for October 17. It will include block parties, rallies, and walks to the polls. But the lessons from these mobilizations have started to shift tactics to include large economic disruptions. Today’s resistance movement recognizes that one-off weekend protests aren’t enough. Unions are powerful members of a resistance coalition not only because they are robust voter turnout operations but more importantly because they can channel the structural power of workers in key industries to grind the system to a halt. In January, when Trump sent a swarm of federal agents into the Twin Cities on a rampage, he lit a match to the tinder that unions and community groups had been laying through decades of coalition work. People’s resistance spread into school walkouts, sit-ins, demonstrations, and strikes. “We modeled our ‘ICE Out’ work similarly to how we prepare to go on strike — leaders in each building and regional leads who work together to cover the city,” said St Paul educator Mara Solis. “Each school had parent captains to work with our educator captains.” These escalating actions grew into a mass uprising that nearly shut down a large metro area. Federal agents beat a retreat from the terror spectacles in Twin Cities streets after January 23, when at least one hundred thousand people marched through Downtown Minneapolis and nearly one million across the state skipped work to participate in a massive political strike, including nonunion construction workers and restaurant workers who called out from popular downtown venues and supermarkets. It showed how, when unions act like movement organizations, nonunion workers can join them in common cause, which is necessary in a country where 90 percent of the population working for a private sector employer earns a living in a nonunion workplace. If the Twin Cities offered an example of layer after layer of society erupting into open rebellion, how can that be replicated nationally? We already have a rendezvous date for massive economic disruption in the months leading up to the next presidential election. Durable Organization May 2028 might still seem like a long time from now, given the urgency of the current crises. But as we witnessed with Black Lives Matter protests, it took years for grassroots activism to culminate in a major wave of protests, with effects that went on resonating for years more. With union contracts set to expire in a presidential year, there’s an opening to coordinate bold demands and worker action to defend democracy, as well as to win economic gains. Workers can put pressure on their employers to call for free and open elections. They can build broad alliances to pressure the state and employers for strong pensions , Medicare for All , a shorter workweek , and taxing the rich . In times of crisis, new organizations can spring up like Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) tents in disaster areas and fold away just as quickly until the next crisis. But movement-building isn’t the same thing as crisis management. To win real change and defend it, you have to keep applying pressure over years; that takes durable organizations that become rooted in people’s lives. The May Day Strong coalition of unions and grassroots organizations, formed in March 2025, is organizing under the banner of “workers over billionaires” to concentrate resistance efforts on the tech oligarchs who prop up Trump’s MAGA coalition and to defend the vote ahead of the midterm and presidential elections. This coalition could take the lessons from the Twin Cities and spread them nationwide. If some unions strike together, other union and nonunion workers can join in other ways, like using sickouts and disruptions to shut things down. Workers at airports and other key economic nodes might have to skip work if they find “abnormally dangerous” working conditions. This level of mass organizing will require unions spending down their vast financial reserves to support workers without union strike funds, which could include legal defense funds and mutual aid networks. If your union has bargaining this year or next, it might not be realistic to line up your contract to expire again in 2028. But one possibility is organizing to win sympathy strike language that permits union workers to honor each other’s picket lines. Article 9 of the Teamsters National Master Freight Agreement and other Teamster contracts offer a model to emulate. Standing Up to Trump Meanwhile, Republicans are launching fishing expeditions against unions backing President Trump’s political opponents . The initial targets of Department of Homeland Security spying and subpoenas of financial records were Minnesota unions plus the Communications Workers of America (CWA) and the Service Employees International Union (SEIU). Now, according to to The Guardian , House Republicans are also investigating the American Federation of Teachers, the United Auto Workers, SMART Transportation Division, and two railroad arms of the Teamsters: the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen, and the Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees Division. And Trump is threatening the integrity of the November elections. The May Day Strong coalition is holding 750 “Solidarity Schools” and actions from late August through mid-September nationwide, bringing together labor organizers and community members to confront the authoritarian threat we face. The trainings are geared toward equipping people with the tools to conduct election defense. Participants learn how to monitor poll sites, and they play out scenarios for how we could respond if federal agents and others attempt to undermine democratic elections through deception, disruption, or suppression of the vote. The scale of action the labor movement will be able to muster on May Day 2028 depends on the organizing we do now.

articles.title: American Reality Is Beyond Parody, but Satire Isn’t Dead
articles.author: Michael G. Vann
articles.content: A specter is haunting contemporary American satire: the specter of reality. This specter poses an existential threat to comedy as social critique. How do you make jokes in this era of hyperabsurdity? Donald Trump’s two administrations sandwiched four years of Joe Biden mumbling incoherently as he stumbling around. Corporations speak in the language of therapy, and airlines charge passengers for micro-comforts while advertising travel as an expression of personal freedom. Billionaires promise to colonize Mars while American cities see their bridges collapse. Streamers make a career out of broadcasting themselves gambling, eating, fighting, shopping, hurling insults, and slowly losing their minds. Kash Patel exists. The late Roman spectacle of a physically repulsive imperial leader planning a massive triumphal arch to honor himself, staging gladiatorial fights for his birthday on his palace lawn, and waging a futile war on Persia. Although Cory Doctorow coined the term “enshittification” to refer to the decay of user experience on online platforms, it now seems applicable to everything. What is the left-leaning comedic artist to do in such conditions? Capitalist Realism Ever in the vanguard, the Chapo Trap House podcast faced this crisis in their first year of existence. From their debut in March 2016, they focused their “dirtbag left” comedic ire on centrist Democrats. During their first live election show in November 2016, they were distraught at Trump’s victory — perhaps not because it harbored a new age of fascism, but because the show’s business model was supposed to be based on dunking on Hiliary Clinton’s neoliberal shit show. Nevertheless, the Chapos persisted and succeeded. With a decade as one of Patreon’s highest-earning podcasts under their belt, they are moving into other media including comic books and now film. Chunks , the new comedy anthology assembled by Chapo Trap House ’s orbit of comedians, podcasters, and filmmakers, offers one compelling answer to 2026’s satire crisis: stop trying to exaggerate America; reproduce its surreal texture and follow its natural absurdities. The result is a hilarious and unsettling ninety-minute journey into the darkness of the American soul. Produced through ColdFeet Films, the production outfit spearheaded by longtime Chapo contributor Amber A’Lee Frost , Chunks consists of six comedy shorts joined by interstitial appearances from Ruby McCollister as a fading Hollywood starlet turned Elvira wannabe public access host out of Bakersfield, California. Its contributors include Sandy Honig, members of Podcast About List and Episode One , Cum Town creator Nick Mullen, Saul Crinier, Nate Fisher, Will Sennett, Michael Cavadias, and Pierce Campion. Chunks moves between animation, live stream aesthetics, public access television, and conventional narrative filmmaking. It’s the jumble of forms appropriate to a country whose citizens increasingly experience reality through competing screens, but also hearkens back to alternative comedy projects such as 1977’s Kentucky Fried Movie and Spike and Mike’s Sick and Twisted Festival of Animation , which toured art house cinemas in the 1990s, as well as Tales from the Crypt and The Twilight Zone . Held together by McCollister’s outstanding performance, Chunks riffs on late night UHF and then cable television from a bygone era, when viewers flipping channels after midnight might stumble upon a deranged local commercial, a public access eccentric, an old movie, an evangelical preacher, or something whose provenance was completely mysterious. The filmmakers invoke that lost world of public access weirdness. Some of the funniest lines are Amber A’Lee Frost’s off-camera banter with the production crew. Those poor interns are probably still editing. Stranger Things But Chunks is not really nostalgic. Its great achievement is recognizing that the disappearance of the old television ecosystem did not make American culture less strange. It made strangeness more centralized, more commercial, and more difficult to escape. The weird guy who once had a half-hour program on channel 63 now has three million followers. The local crank has become a content creator. The public access psychic has become a wellness influencer. The infomercial has conquered the culture so completely that much of ordinary life now possesses the rhythm of an advertisement. Chunks works with this brave new world. Its six segments (“Utopia Air,” “The Eater,” “Office of Tomorrow,” “Poker Night at the Pleasure Trove,” “Charming Bears,” and “You Should Feel Better”) sound like channels encountered while insomnia pushes you deeper into the television dial. Yet their collective subject is recognizably twenty-first-century America: consumption, work, entertainment, technological mediation, therapeutic language, and the bizarre psychological compromises required to survive institutions nobody particularly believes in anymore. The anthology format works so well because contemporary America lacks a coherent narrative. It feels like scrolling. One moment you are watching footage from Gaza. The next you are being shown an advertisement for sports gambling. Then somebody is explaining their trauma. Then a senator is yelling about declining masculinity. Then DoorDash informs you that your burrito is approaching. Then a billionaire explains that artificial intelligence will liberate humanity from work. Then your employer emails to announce a mandatory seminar on resilience. Then you learn that the most powerful military in global history, which has recently murdered over 150 schoolgirls, will be giving the troops testosterone injections to create a “High-T” fighting force. Chunks reproduces this fragmentation without simply imitating the internet. Its world is recognizably downstream from television, advertising, podcasts, animation, live streaming, and algorithmic culture, but the film’s comedy comes from placing these forms next to one another until their shared pathology becomes visible. The Casino Economy Take the very idea of “Poker Night at the Pleasure Trove,” organized around a live streamed poker game, complete with a lively comments section (take the time to pause the video and read these). Gambling may be one of the perfect cultural forms of contemporary America, as the economy increasingly resembles a casino, while the casino increasingly presents itself as an economy. Sports broadcasts are saturated with betting lines, and cryptocurrency transformed financial speculation into mass entertainment. Ordinary people are encouraged to conceive of security not through wages, pensions, public services, or unions but through investments, side hustles, and improbable jackpots. Despite the fact that young men are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of online gambling, the gaming industry buys off cash-starved public universities and turns student athlete uniforms into casino advertisements . Chunks finds morbid humor in how America has transformed risk into leisure because it has already transformed ordinary life into risk. Something similar hangs over the anthology’s take on corporate culture. An animated segment about the private lives of adorable commercial mascots, Nick Mullen’s “Charming Bears,” takes beings created entirely for advertising and asks us to imagine the psychic existence beneath their synthetic smiles. The absurd premise gets at something fundamental about contemporary culture. We inhabit a society crowded with friendly corporate personalities. Insurance companies have mascots, and fast-food chains have personalities. Brands make jokes on social media and undergo carefully scripted moral awakenings. These days, capital doesn’t just want our money; it wants a relationship. Mullen’s bears poke at the nightmare of corporate domination dressed as intimacy. However, his comedic genius takes us deep into the lives of these cartoon bears and finds that they share our existential crises, face all too familiar financial precarity, and ultimately find solace in a quixotic act of defiance that is equally scatological as it is emotionally resonant. Feeling Better Contributor Sandy Honig proves herself to be a triple threat, writing, directing, and starring in “Utopia Air.” While most of this installment does a spectacular job of lampooning the host of indignities that commercial airlines call “service,” she highjacks the narrative and flies us into the forbidden airspace of transcendental knowledge. Despite moments of horror, Honig assures us that the trip is going to be just fine. “The Eater,” the work of Patrick Doran, Cameron Fetter, and Caleb Pitts, is a horror mystery that leaves the viewer with more questions than answers. Its atmosphere and critique of consumerism resonate with the best aspects of Fight Club on commodity fetishism. The final segment’s title, “You Should Feel Better,” could serve as a motto for the current political economic order. America has become extraordinarily proficient at converting social problems into psychological ones. You are not overworked; you need mindfulness. You are not underpaid; you need financial literacy. You are not isolated because public life has been hollowed out; you need to practice self-care. You do not despise your job because work has become degrading and insecure; you need to find your purpose. This is the ultimate neoliberal command: adjust yourself. Chunks belongs to an older tradition of American left-wing comedy, even though it avoids delivering anything resembling a conventional political lecture. Its politics reside in its eye for quotidian humiliations. The America depicted here is ridiculous because its institutions continually demand that people participate sincerely in situations that are manifestly insane. That is also why Chapo Trap House turns out to be a surprisingly natural incubator for a film project. Since its emergence during the 2016 election, Chapo ’s best comedy has depended less on conventional joke construction than on noticing the ideological content embedded in apparently trivial cultural objects: campaign advertisements, bad newspaper columns, superhero movies, conservative Facebook posts, airport bookstores, LinkedIn language, mediocre restaurants, and the endless artifacts produced by an empire trying desperately to entertain itself as it sinks further into decline and decadence. Underground Variety Show Crucially, however, the film does not feel like a filmed podcast. The filmmakers and producers care about filmmaking. This is hardly surprising, as cinema is a constant reference point on Chapo and Will Menaker has an ongoing series called Movie Mindset . The anthology deliberately changes visual languages, including animation, public access pastiche, live stream presentation, and narrative shorts. The result is closer to an underground variety show than branded bonus content. Even people involved with the production have emphasized the diversity of form across the segments, while ColdFeet’s stated ambition was to provide resources for comedians and filmmakers to make larger projects in a style increasingly absent from conventional television. That matters politically as well as aesthetically. American entertainment has undergone the same process of consolidation that has affected the rest of the economy. Gigantic corporations spend enormous sums producing material designed to offend nobody, surprise nobody, and remain permanently available as intellectual property. Streaming promised unlimited choice and delivered menus containing thousands of nearly interchangeable objects. Algorithms, not artistic visions, determine cinema culture. Meanwhile, the economically precarious weirdos who historically made American comedy interesting are told to produce clips. Chunks offers a modest alternative: give funny people enough resources to make something strange. This delightfully utopian gesture will throw Generation X viewers into nostalgic melancholy. This is what punk was supposed to be. Let a hundred flowers bloom. The film’s satire is consequently more affectionate than nihilistic. Beneath all the grotesquerie is a conviction that people themselves remain funny, inventive, sociable, and worth watching. What deserves contempt are the systems into which they have been inserted. Shopping for America This distinction is increasingly important. Plenty of contemporary comedy gazes upon American stupidity and concludes that Americans are stupid. Chunks suggests something more interesting. People behave strangely because the world around them has become strange. They gamble because security has disappeared; they retreat into screens because public life has withered. They speak corporate nonsense because employment requires it. They consume endlessly because, ever since President George W. Bush told us to fight al-Qaeda by “shopping more,” citizenship has been reconceived as consumption. In America, reality has become impossible to parody because the absurdity is structural. This makes Chunks more than an entertaining collection of sketches. The film captures America in the peculiar phase when decline has ceased to feel exceptional and become an aesthetic, even though we can vaguely remember an era when things were less awful. Everything still works, more or less. The planes still fly, the apps still load, the office still opens. The shelves in CVS are stocked most of the time, but not fully. The commercial mascot continues smiling, and the live stream continues streaming. Somebody somewhere is always telling us that things are getting better, even though we have those intrusive memories of life not being so bad. As the tradition of all dead broadcasts weighs like a nightmare on the brains of the living, let’s hope that somewhere after midnight, Ruby McCollister is still in front of the camera, introducing the next offering from Chunks .

articles.title: France’s Left Faces the 2027 Election Divided
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content: Over Christmastime 2018, Jean-Luc Mélenchon met for lunch with Raphaël Glucksmann in France’s National Assembly. Mélenchon was an MP at the time, fresh off his strong 2017 presidential run for France Insoumise. Glucksmann was a liberal essayist with a murky background advising sometimes-dubious politicians in countries like Ukraine and Georgia, producing documentaries about human rights issues while looking to get into politics himself. The conversation stayed light and nonconfrontational, and they were joined by the former Socialist Emmanuel Maurel (at that time supportive of France Insoumise), and Thomas Porcher, an economist who’d voted for Mélenchon the year before. Porcher would go on to cofound Glucksmann’s new electoral outfit, called Place Publique, later that year. This new formation, Porcher told Le Monde at the time, was not founded to be “anti–Jean-Luc Mélenchon.” A decade on, though — and just eight months ahead of the 2027 presidential election — it’s hard to believe that’s true. Today hard-liners like Glucksmann and his wing of the Left have ruled out any potential alliance with Mélenchon, whether it’s in the presidential race or the parliamentary contest held directly afterward. This position raises the stakes for the Parti Socialiste primary, which will be held in mid-October. Once the leading force on the Left, the Socialists were in power between 1981–95 and 2012–17. Today the party is substantially weaker, but it’s still an electoral factor, and the primary will determine exactly what role it plays. Some contenders, like Maurel, favor unity on the Left. Glucksmann’s camp, however, pushed hard in the other direction, unsuccessfully arguing in favor of a written ban on any alliance with France Insoumise, today France’s largest left-wing party. Glucksmann’s Place Publique views Mélenchon as an antisemite, a “friend of Putin,” and a would-be autocrat. The glory days of the broad left-wing electoral alliances of 2022 and 2024 are over, and not everybody thinks that’s a bad thing. Others, though, worry it could cost the Left the presidency and even bring the far right to power. Broad Left In 2027, one thing is sure: there will be more than one candidate running for president on the Left. The Parti Communiste Français (PCF) designated its general secretary, Fabien Roussel, as its candidate in early September; the Parti Socialiste primary in which Glucksmann is running will choose a contender in the middle of next month; and another major force on the Left, the Greens, are still debating whether it’s appropriate to run their own candidate at all. “This is a unique presidential election,” the consensus-seeking president of the Greens’ parliamentary group Cyrielle Chatelain told me. “We could see the far right come to power, so we’re reflecting on what the best way is to present our ideas in this context.” In 2022, an electoral alliance spanning the broad Left denied Emmanuel Macron a governing majority, leading to parliamentary instability throughout his second presidential term. Despite the electoral success, the pact soon broke up over friction between France Insoumise and the other left-wing parties. Another alliance was forged for the 2024 snap parliamentary elections. Every poll and pundit ( including myself ) predicted the election would sweep Marine Le Pen’s far-right Rassemblement National into power. In 2024, that alliance, dubbed the Nouveau Front Populaire, as well as strategic stand-down deals with candidates from the center, delayed the far right’s march to power. But this alliance also quickly fell apart. Grievances over the political style and positions of Mélenchon and France Insoumise — in particular centered on unfounded allegations of antisemitism, in the context of Israel’s escalating genocide in Palestine — authored the demise of the left-wing front. Even still, this spring’s municipal elections saw alliances between left-wing forces. Many included France Insoumise, as in Saint-Denis where its joint list with the PCF won the election in the first round, or in cities like Grenoble and Lyon, where alliances including France Insoumise kept the mayor’s office in the Left’s hands. With Mélenchon now the Left’s front-runner in the presidential race, these parties are questioning what to do. Should these parties support Mélenchon and France Insoumise, despite their harsh criticisms of his party? Or should they run candidates who have little chance of making the runoff, and risk taking enough from Mélenchon’s score to ensure no left-winger makes the decisive second-round contest? And if Le Pen wins, will the Left unite, even around France Insoumise, if it’s the only chance of stopping her governing with a crushing parliamentary majority? Revolution Fabien Roussel’s coronation as the PCF’s candidate earlier this month came as no surprise. The PCF congress voted 72 percent in favor of rerunning their 2022 candidate, despite a current within the party called Alternative Communiste arguing that running him last election did nothing to staunch the party’s decline . “A communist candidate must allow us to rebuild our influence and to reestablish national visibility,” Alternative Communiste wrote ahead of the party congress vote. “[In 2022 our candidate Roussel] got 2.28 percent of the vote. Five years later, nothing allows us to think that a new candidature will fundamentally change the balance of power.” For these internal critics, it was important to recognize how “recent events. . . . have demonstrated that the most reactionary forces are converging.. . . . in 2027, it’s communists’ responsibility to contribute to putting forward a joint candidate who is capable of winning.” Some on the Left are not running to win. Small Trotskyist groupings like Lutte ouvrière or Révolution permanente have also named candidates, but they rarely get more than 1 percent of the vote. François Ruffin, a former France Insoumise lawmaker who dramatically broke with the party after winning reelection in 2024, is also running, though he has danced around with allying with the Parti Socialiste. He’s even reportedly flirted with an alliance with Dominique de Villepin — a conservative former prime minister who’s spoken out strongly about Israel’s genocide in Palestine and is considering his own cross-party bid. These candidates of the radical and revolutionary left once represented around 15 percent of the vote, before Mélenchon established electoral hegemony over similar voters. In 2012 and 2017, the PCF joined forces and supported Mélenchon’s runs, but the majority of the party’s voting membership no longer supports this. Despite the PCF’s serious policy differences with France Insoumise — including its support for nuclear energy and rejection of Mélenchon’s narrative on racism — the party has often voted with France Insoumise and the Greens to censure Macron’s governments. Reform The two candidates who best represent the Parti Socialiste’s divisions are its first secretary Olivier Faure and Glucksmann, who Faure recruited to lead its list in the 2024 EU elections. Glucksmann proposes reorienting the French left toward a more emphatic pro-EU line with paeans to democracy, human rights, and reindustrializing the EU. The aim: to head off both Russian imperialism and the Communist Party of China slyly taking over the world through trade. Wherever Mélenchon and Glucksmann occasionally still intersect on policy, Glucksmann quickly backs off. In a recent polemic following Mélenchon’s proposition to cancel some of France’s debt held by the European Central Bank, the president of Glucksmann’s party claimed that now isn’t the time for such a move — despite previously supporting it. A Glucksmann victory in the primary would amount to a referendum against any alliance with Mélenchon or France Insoumise. Always wary of France Insoumise’s hegemony over the Left, this week 292 leading figures and power brokers in the Parti Socialiste signed a letter calling for a Glucksmann vote. His main rival is Faure, who took charge of the Parti Socialiste after its electoral collapse in 2017, when it won just 6 percent of the presidential vote. In 2022, its vote fell below 2 percent. However, for Arthur Delaporte, an MP for Calvados who’s close to Faure, the party’s first secretary is the natural candidate representing left-wing unity — and who’s running on his record as the “artisan” of recent broad-left alliances. A Faure presidency, Delaporte told me, would look much different from the record of the last Socialist president, François Hollande, in 2012–17. On labor, Delaporte says, Faure would depart from the former president’s example of weakening worker power in the labor code. Delaporte cited rolling back the “inversion of the hierarchy of norms” — a reference to a provision in Hollande’s reform which allowed branches of companies to negotiate conditions worse than those already agreed at the company level. The pro-business argument behind the “inversion” was that it could give companies more space to maneuver in a constrained business environment. Unions warned that companies would use it to “blackmail” union negotiations by threatening layoffs unless workers accepted a worse deal. Delaporte also pointed to rolling back unemployment insurance changes under Hollande and Macron as a priority. In this primary, Philippe Brun — an MP from Eure — tried to distinguish himself by calling for changing France’s retirement system to capitalization. It’s a measure supported by the center and the Right, all of whose candidates have called for such change to France’s redistributive system. Brun repeated right-wing arguments that there are no longer enough active workers to fund pensions. But on September 16, Brun was excluded from the party and its primary after allegations arose of violence against a parliamentary assistant, which he denies. On capitalization at least, Mélenchon and Faure are aligned. “We will never pass to a system of retirement by capitalization,” thundered Mélenchon in one speech to supporters, arguing that individually paid-for retirement plans would require much higher contributions, and that market instability could delay or wipe out workers’ retirements. Is Faure open to capitalization? I asked Delaporte. “No, that’s not one of the themes we’ve defended,” he replied. Popular Greens During the Paris municipal elections this spring, a small group of local politicians broke from the Greens’ official alliance with the Parti Socialiste and formed the Verts Populaires, which supported France Insoumise. Some were purged from the party, but their current is growing, with the Greens anchoring themselves more firmly on the Left over the past five years. However, other Greens are moving away from the radical left. At a Glucksmann r ally in June, the Greens’ 2022 presidential candidate Yannick Jadot told reporters that Mélenchon isn’t the candidate he wants leading the Left. Jadot quickly joined Glucksmann’s campaign after he entered the race last month. But some Green politicians see Mélenchon as having a better chance of winning than any other left-wing candidate. Sandrine Rousseau, runner-up in the Greens’ leadership election in 2023, has openly criticized the party leadership’s ambiguity on pursuing an alliance with France Insoumise and criticized talks to ally with other sections of the Left instead. “I don’t know what the non-Mélenchonist left is, because we don’t really know what their proposals or main principles are,” Rousseau said in August. Chatelain, the head of the Green parliamentary group, is reportedly in favor of an alliance with Mélenchon. She appeared alongside him as a guest at France Insoumise’s summer conference, with Le Canard enchaîné reporting that Jadot believes she’s made her choice and is just waiting for the right time to announce a decision. Chatelain told me that for now there are no formal or informal discussions between the Greens and other parties about a presidential alliance; she was coy about what choice the party should make, deferring to the democratic desires of the membership. She said that any presidential campaign the Greens joined would have to have a strong ecological program, ending fossil-fuel usage and transitioning to 100 percent renewable energy. Still she added that she doesn’t talk in terms of programmatic red lines, given that France’s left has campaigned jointly twice in recent elections and each time succeeded in reconciling its differences. “I don’t think there are any insurmountable issues on the Left,” she said. Grand Coalition While many on the Left are still weighing the best path to take, centrists see winning part of them over as a necessary step to avoid a Le Pen presidency. Clément Beaune and Philippe Grangeon, two early-hour Macronists, argued earlier this month that a grand coalition should be organized even before next spring’s election. “Excluded, of course, are the two extremes; those on the Right who make the rule of law a scapegoat, and those on the Left who have never excluded a compromise with France Insoumise,” Beaune and Grangeon wrote. Of particular worry, they say, is the Rassemblement National’s plan to halve France’s contribution to the EU ahead of negotiations for the bloc’s 2028–34 budget, claiming that “Europe. . . . [is] the only space of effective sovereignty in the twenty-first century.” Former President Hollande believes he could be a candidate of last resort for this camp, if no consensus is established by the winter. Speaking on a radio show in early September, he argued that if a candidate wants to make it to the second round, they have to not only be capable of rallying the Left but also conscious of the need to reach beyond their own political family. “Does that mean potentially governing with the center?” “Yes!” Hollande exclaimed. “It’s maybe the best manner, this broad coalition, to have the stability to transform, to act.” Hollande has struggled to reach double digits in polling scenarios that count him as a candidate. While at the start of his presidency he headed a broad left-wing coalition with a huge majority, by the time he left office in 2017 his approval rating fluttered above the bottom of the Mariana Trench at 4 percent. The fact that he is today seeking allies on the Right and in the center is proof that France’s left has learned the error of his ways. The question that remains is whether it can build a principled alliance of its own.

articles.title: Debating Victor Serge
articles.author: Mitchell Abidor
articles.content: When I began writing Victor Serge: Unruly Revolutionary , I expected to write a biography in keeping with the image common on the left of Serge as an uncompromising enemy of Stalinism who never fell into anti-communism and fought all his life for revolutionary socialism. This is what we find in the many writings of Richard Greeman, who single-handedly rescued Serge from oblivion by translating his novels and tirelessly writing about him. In fact, my biography began as a collaboration between me and Richard, one we abandoned due to differences in interpretation. Suzi Weissman presents that image as well in her biography of Serge, The Course Is Set on Hope . A fuller account of this Serge was what I thought I was going to write. Things did not turn out that way. I worked mainly from primary sources from archives around the world as well as long-forgotten newspapers and magazines for which Serge wrote. What I found was a man far different from the one we find in Greeman’s and Weissman’s books (and all those who draw from their work) but also the one Serge presented in his justly famous Memoirs of a Revolutionary, 1901–1941 . I found a man who ceaselessly evolved politically, which I found admirable. But the evolution I found went in directions even I was shocked to find: that Serge was a man who came to believe in his final years that socialist revolution was no longer in the cards, and that those who believed it were frozen in the past. I was also shocked to discover in his correspondence, articles, and notebooks that Serge became an anti-communist and in certain regards an apologist for the West in the early days of the Cold War. There was no denying the evidence, and everything I wrote is documented in my book. I knew I’d upset people, and I offered to debate some of those I told of my discoveries. I was never offered the chance to do so, and the recently published critique of me and my findings first appeared in several European publications and now in English in Jacobin . To fully respond to the attack by Suzi Weissman, Carlo Albertani, and Christian Dubucq on Victor Serge: Unruly Revolutionary , I would have to quote the entire book. I respond here, however briefly and incompletely. An example of their hasty and incorrect reading is their claim that I imply Serge was a police spy at the time of the Liabeuf Affair. The trio writes that “Abidor notes that the socialist journalist Gustave Hervé was prosecuted for public statements, whereas Serge was not. Although he acknowledges that no documentary evidence explains why Serge escaped prosecution, he nevertheless invites the reader to infer that his immunity reflected dubious dealings with the police.” I wrote or implied nothing of the sort, and what I said is unambiguous. In fact, I very specifically said that in writing about the Liabeuf case, “Gustave Hervé took a similar tack [to that of Serge], and in fact used many of the same words that Serge would a couple of weeks later. It is indicative of the relative threat posed by Hervé and Serge that, though they wrote the same things, Hervé went to jail for his opinions while Serge went undisturbed by the police.” Yes, I note Serge went undisturbed by the police, but I clearly say that this was because he was not a threat, while the well-known Hervé was. How this can be read as an accusation that Serge was a police informant is a mystery. I’m not even certain they read the book. My critics write, “As an anarchist, one might reasonably have expected Abidor’s criticism to focus on Serge’s decision to join the Bolshevik Party in 1919, marking his break with the anarchism of his youth. But this is not the case.” Had they actually read the book, they would have seen that the lengthiest and densest chapter is on Serge’s dishonesty about the Soviet Union in his writings on the new state and anarchism. I make the case that Serge lied when writing propaganda pieces for the international Communist press. In these articles, he claimed that the USSR was the fulfillment of the anarchist dream. As I show, using contemporary accounts in the anarchist press by anarchists from several countries who met Serge in Moscow in the early 1920s, Serge privately told his former comrades that the Soviet state was awful, while writing articles that claimed the opposite and encouraged anarchists to join him there. This is part of a chapter in which I also detail the Bolsheviks’ brutal and underhanded war on anarchists and anarchism. I will plead guilty to one thing that this group didn’t bring up. I attempt to explain why Serge might have knowingly written falsehoods. Is this an incidence of the “psychologizing” I’m attacked for? I look at this matter from many angles, all sympathetic to Serge, who was truly in a bind. Anarchists have told me that Serge’s conduct was inexcusable, and that my search for extenuating circumstances was unacceptable: lies are lies, and leading anarchists to move to the USSR was leading them to their deaths. Sometimes a biographer just can’t win. Weissman and her friends write, “Abidor treats the anarcho-individualist movement, in which Serge was an active participant for nearly a decade, with scant sympathy.” This is absurd. I would have hoped that people who admire Serge would be aware that I translated and edited Anarchists Never Surrender , a collection of Serge’s anarchist writings in 2015, the first and only one of its kind in English. That book is an admiring one, and in both that volume, the biography, and two other books I’ve dedicated to French individualist anarchism, I defend this tradition that Serge once so ably represented. I do subject the school to lengthy analysis and draw some critical conclusions, but that’s not a sign of “scant sympathy”; it’s proof I take it seriously. Had my critics actually read every page of Unruly Revolutionary , they’d have seen that I also note and criticize Serge’s harsh treatment of anarchist individualism in his novel The Birth of Our Power . I even located and approvingly quoted the review of that book by his former coeditor of the anarchist paper L’Anarchie and first wife, Rirette Maîtrejean, who condemned her former companion for the way he had “evolved’ and for his “disdain” for his former individualist anarchist comrades. In any case, criticizing my treatment of anarchism is odd coming from Weissman, who dedicated three pages to Serge’s anarchism in her book on him, none of it showing any familiarity with Serge’s writings in French. Credit where credit is due, Carlo Albertani is not guilty of this error in the first volume of his biography of Serge, published in France last year. Serge’s ideas evolved greatly over the course of his life, and his attachment to revolutionary socialism took a blow during and especially after World War II. He grew increasingly exasperated with his fellow left-wing anti-Stalinist exiles in Mexico, who thought World War II would end in revolutions, just as World War I had. He turned his back on Marxist orthodoxy and denied that possibility. I write about this approvingly and at length in the chapter “The Revolution Revised.” The working class, in his eyes, had suffered an enormous defeat and was not in a state to carry out revolution. In this book and in my other writings on Serge, I have praised him for this change in point of view. He wrote extensively of his shift in his Notebooks , and I highly recommend that anyone who hasn’t already read that essential volume do so. In it, we find this diagnosis by Serge of the politics of the revolutionary socialists among his fellow exiles: “Their extremely optimistic and schematic conviction that the Russian Revolution will soon be repeated in Europe. ‘The workers will occupy the factories (Pivert), they’ll take power (Gironella), etc.’ So deluded are they that the POUMists think that they’ll be back in a free, socialist Spain in six months, and Pivert speaks proudly of the potential for the formation of a Red Army in France!” All of this revolutionary sloganeering was detached from reality, and Serge told his comrades just that and did so bluntly. The final years of Serge’s Notebooks are full of evidence supporting the case for Serge’s abandonment of the “revolutionary” in revolutionary socialism. So bad had things become that Serge was informed in a letter that “the comrades of POUM . . . and Marceau [Pivert], Stein, and Jacob unanimously consider that, for ideological and political reasons, collaboration with you is impossible.” It’s certainly not by chance that Weissman and her friends refer only to the French edition of the book, which is an essential and impressive piece of work. To speak of it as Serge’s Notebooks , published by New York Review Books, would require that they acknowledge that the translator, who would necessarily know precisely what is contained in a book that details Serge’s evolution was . . . me. The immediate postwar period proved Serge right about revolution and permanently soured his relationship with the revolutionary left. His ignoble physical fight with fellow exile Jean Malaquais in 1944 was over the latter’s accusation that Serge called for an alliance with the Tories. This was an exaggeration of Serge’s actual position, since he hoped for a “socialist-leaning” future, but Serge was in no way a revolutionary socialist at the end of the war and in his final years. As I show, in his final interview, coincidentally published the day he died, he nowhere even mentioned socialism. His primary concern, one that recurs in his public and private writings, which I discovered in his archives, was the protection of the human person. Personalism had become his guiding philosophy. Victor Serge, the Anti-Communist My most controversial claim is that Serge was an anti-communist, for which I provide ample evidence, too ample to lay out here. I don’t speculate about what his future direction would have been. I wrote, “To say Serge would have evolved in the same directions as his comrade in anti-Stalinism Boris Souvarine, who eventually supported the US in Vietnam, might be going too far. But it’s hard to deny, given the positions he took and the language he employed in expressing his opinions . . . that Serge agreed with the point of view of ex-communist anti-communists like Arthur Koestler.” I spoke only of where he was, not where he might have gone. And where he was was obsessive anti-communism. A large chunk of the book is dedicated to this period and this phase in Serge’s political evolution. To spell everything out would extend this response to dozens of pages. My claim is not based solely on his writing for the anti-communist press, like the liberal anti-communist New Leader . His private correspondence is replete with references to “reds” and “commies.” He considered communism “the worst danger, a mortal danger” to humanity, more of a danger than the West, which he considered a benign, even positive force. Weissman and co. argue he wrote for the anti-communist New Leader because the communists blocked him from publishing elsewhere. Were the communists really that powerful everywhere that they could sway publishers at will? As I ask in the book, how is it that the French Communists were unable to block Koestler from publishing Darkness at Noon , which appeared with no difficulty and to great success? No less a figure than Dwight MacDonald , as I show in my book, warned Serge against the path he was taking. His correspondence with Emmanuel Mounier, the brilliant philosopher and founder of the variant of personalism to which Serge adhered, is filled with anti-communist screeds and attacks on Mounier for being soft on communism. When Serge died, Mounier wrote, “Since the war his letters were polarized around a single concern: the Soviet dictatorship and the camps in the USSR. . . . Far from France, he spoke inaccurately of realities he didn’t know. But we forgive him this, for men of his mettle and humanity are few.” Serge also suffered from the paranoia of a Cold Warrior, seeing the communist hand everywhere, particularly within the United States and its government. In a 1940 letter, he wrote, “I know that the Stalinist work is being done in the United States on a large scale by a goodly number of journalists, and Stalinist intellectuals who have arrived there. They even have a certain amount of support in the Administration. . . . Their action is and will be camouflaged. . . . They would do anything to get all their personnel installed in the United States.” Elucubrations like these are clearly the work of an anti-communist or, to phrase it better, a premature Cold Warrior. See this quote from a 1946 essay in a collection of Serge’s articles called The New Russian Imperialism . I wrote in the biography: He downplayed the threat and even importance of Western imperialism. In that publication he insisted that the British Empire, led by the Labour government, “is evacuating from Egypt and offers India its independence. The old methods of colonial exploitation are exhausted.” As for the exemplar of the new form of imperialism, the United States, Serge claimed that he “knew Americans sufficiently well to know that they don’t contemplate imposing tyrannies on the five continents and on the contrary desire a sustainable reorganization of international relations.” Leaving aside how poor this all was as a prediction, especially as regards America, this is hardly revolutionary socialism, which I think we can all agree would be anti-imperialist. The “exhaustion of the old imperialisms” Serge spoke of didn’t prohibit France from fighting for years to hold on to Indochina and Algeria. The Mau Maus of Kenya would have been surprised to learn that England was gladly setting their colonies free. Weissman and co. omit any mention of Serge’s 1947 letter to André Malraux, in which Serge says that if he were in France, he would have voted for de Gaulle. Though his son claimed the letter was a fake, there’s no reason to think it was, and the sentiments it expresses are in keeping with his beliefs at the time. He so hated communists and communism that he would have been willing to support France’s main barrier to Communist victory in France’s elections. This shocked the revolutionary left of the time, none of whom cast any doubt on the reality of this letter or Serge’s authorship. Two final things: As I did with Weissman and Richard Greeman, whose lifelong work on Serge I benefited from, I informed Birchall while I was writing the book of the conclusions I was reaching. He expressed his disagreement, and before reading the book told me that my thesis was incorrect. Ian and I disagree about many things, but he is an honorable man. He read the book with an open mind and was convinced by what I had to say about Serge’s anti-communism. Ian is a lifetime Trotskyist and a respected scholar and activist. The baseness of Weissman and her friends is revealed by their attack on him for being convinced by my documentation. Suzi Weissman has held fast over the years to a mythical version of Victor Serge, revolutionary socialist sans peur et sans reproche, one that was also propagated by my friend and mentor, Richard Greeman. I did not start writing Victor Serge: Unruly Revolutionary thirteen years ago as the critical volume it turned out to be. It was my reading of his anarchist writings, which contradicted his claims in his memoirs about not supporting anarchist illegalism; the transcript of the Bonnot Gang trial; in which his conduct was less than stellar; and what I found in archival sources that led the book to go in an unexpected direction. It was not my “anarchism” that led me to write the book that so displeases those who cling to the myth. It was the facts and, as I say in the introduction, my lack of the phrenological bump for veneration that forced me to write the book I wrote. Serge was at one time a revolutionary socialist, and at one time he wasn’t an anti-communist. He ceased being the former and became the latter in his final years. There’s no shame or surprise in the fact that Serge’s ideas changed with circumstances: that was a constant throughout his life. Let me end by quoting some apposite words of Serge’s concerning his fellow exiles who remained attached to out-of-date schemas. He said they were “idealists hemmed in by the sclerosis of doctrines and circumstances, and dominated by their convictions and their emotional attachments; in short, by fanaticism. Under such conditions the person who disturbs the inner security of the others is a hateful heretic.” Weissman, Albertani, and Dubucq cling to an imaginary Serge, one who fits their political needs and desires. They’re free to believe they’re right, but hagiography is not biography, and facts are stubborn things.

articles.title: Flock Off: How Westland DSA Members Pushed Flock Cameras Out of Their City
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: By filling city council meetings, educating the public on mass surveillance, and cooperating with like-minded allies, DSA members in Westland shot down a Flock contract renewal. By Dave N. and Kathy E. In July 2024 the city of Westland signed up for a trial run with Flock Safety that would last until August 2026. Flock’s cameras are Automated License Plate Readers (ALPR) that mark the date, time, and location where a vehicle passes. Flock claims that its technology does not scan human faces, but its cameras are able to fingerprint cars based on minute details like rust or bumper stickers. The technology is similar to that used in facial recognition software. These services are sold to law enforcement and advertised to cities as a tool for safety (e.g. tracking stolen vehicles or resolving car accidents). In reality, police officers have used this technology to stalk ex-spouses, target women seeking abortions, and aid ICE raids. Given privacy concerns, civil rights, and the actual safety of citizens, it was in the interest of any resident of Westland to shoot Flock down. We learned, however, through hearing from citizens at Westland city council meetings and by talking with council members, that Westland is a very pro-police city. Even with a DSA-endorsed socialist, Mike McDermott, as council president, the majority of the council were convinced by the police department’s arguments for Flock. Upon approval in 2024, ten new Flock poles were placed in the city. In 2025 Metro Detroit DSA began organizing in western Wayne County by forming a geographic working group that became known as Socialists Organizing Western Wayne ( SOWW ). In the beginning, we were learning about one another, how to organize, and even what socialism meant. After six months, we had grown to over 20 members with 15–20 consistently attending meetings. Organizing around the Flock contract turned into our first real project. The group’s main goal was to find a way to guarantee four council votes (a simple majority) against renewing the Flock contract. Elijah Nemr led the anti-Flock campaign. He was a relatively new DSA member who leveraged his technical background to facilitate meetings, organize members, research, and speak at Westland city council meetings and other civic events. Most of the city council members are openly pro-police. Mike was able to guarantee one vote besides his own, from the only Republican, Emily Bauman. Mike’s ability to gather two more votes was hampered by a law prohibiting four or more council members to meet in private. SOWW’s Flock sub-group saw that public pressure was the main way to gather two more votes. Mike proposed two approaches to achieve this pressure, and we executed both: the inside and the outside. The inside approach was to have SOWW members attend city council meetings and speak publicly to council members. We also spoke to the other residents attending the meetings to create public anger and gain more support. The outside approach was for SOWW members to canvass in neighborhoods and distribute petitions to pressure Westland not to renew the contract. While canvassing we learned that most people didn’t understand the difference between Flock cameras and CCTV cameras. CCTV cameras require a warrant or a subpoena to access the footage, while Flock cameras upload information to an unaccountable database that law enforcement can access at any moment. Once we showed examples of police who misused the technology and explained how Flock cameras didn’t require warrants, residents immediately became disturbed and supported our efforts. One of the strongest tactics we used was to leverage a wide array of talking points when addressing city council. We got help on our petitions from our sibling group in Ferndale, the Ferndale Area Organizing Committee (FAOC) , which had successfully pressured Ferndale not to renew its Flock contract. FAOC gave us many resources, literature, and debate strategies that had been effective there. We began forming speeches personal to each Westland resident about why they opposed Flock. For example, we have several mothers in our group and one of them, Liz, decided to highlight the predatory threats Flock cameras posed to children. At a council meeting, she stated: As a parent, I’m deeply concerned about the ever-increasing levels of surveillance our children are being raised to believe is normal. There are many stories emerging of Flock’s inability to keep the sensitive information they collect safe, further raising concerns about this kind of surveillance technology and how it impacts our youth. Liz’s story, along with framing that focused on the safety concern that Flock cameras pose, immediately garnered public support. This video of one public comment session shows Liz and others who spoke about why they oppose surveillance. We allied with the president of the Westland Democratic Club to put more pressure and speak out against Flock to the council. We consulted with independent journalists and collaborated with other organizations such as The People’s Assembly . Peoples’ Assembly and DeFlock (a national open-source project that maps Flock cameras) sent speakers to our council meetings. The first meeting of July showed the fruits of these efforts — instead of SOWW members being the main public commenters on Flock, multiple constituents who had not spoken before on the topic rose to voice their concerns about the cameras. That meeting was the boiling point — within a few days, councilwoman Melissa Sampey posted to Facebook the council’s decision not to renew the contract and to let it expire. Sampey’s post revealed the force behind this decision: “Community Engagement Matters.” SOWW was able to demonstrate that a DSA geographic group can multiply the efforts of our SIOs. Mike McDermott is our only SIO on city council, and SOWW demonstrated that a DSA geographic group can multiply the efforts of our SIOs. We built an issue campaign to create public pressure on elected officials, through a unified group that devoted time to forming relationships with constituents. Attending Westland Democratic Club meetings and Westland cultural events allowed us to create allies, and those allies came out and spoke against Flock. SOWW also cultivated organizing skills, and new members gained memorable organizing experience that they can take beyond the Flock campaign. SOWW trained new organizers to speak publicly, compile literature, and canvas. Growing as an organizer also requires personal development. One of our new members, Kate, said she was “inherently a socially anxious person, but working with such a supportive and motivated group really helped me feel comfortable speaking up.” People are motivated to try things they struggle with when it’s for a greater cause and for others; that’s a core tenet of organizing. The support and camaraderie in SOWW made a space to develop future organizers. And there’s a need for those organizers: our work on ending mass surveillance is far from finished. Inkster, Livonia, Garden City, and Romulus all have Flock contracts. Our group needs to carry this momentum to one of these cities, but we need to decide soon. SOWW was created to organize locally alongside our Socialists in Office (SIOs) — Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib, State Representative Dylan Wegela, and Westland City Council President Mike McDermott — where their districts overlap in Westland, Romulus, Inkster, and Garden City. If you are interested in the work we do, please contact Jill Rossiter, Elijah Nemr (Elijah S), or Kathy Elrick on Slack or fill out our interest form . David N. has been an active member of DSA since July 2025. He is not a part of any caucus. In SOWW he has contributed to power mapping Westland, town hall organizing, and mutual aid. Kathy E. has been an active member of the chapter since 2023 and is co-chair of SOWW. She started hosting DSA coffee socials in western Wayne County in 2024. She is uncaucused and active in starting a local DSA, community garden collaboration in Norwayne, and Mutual Aid 101 and 102 events. Flock Off: How Westland DSA Members Pushed Flock Cameras Out of Their City was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: Stiffing Workers, Rationing Toilet Paper: Who Really Makes WPI Run?
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
