articles.content: Resident Advisors on strike in 2024 take their picket line to Earle Bridge. Worcester DSA members join with a banner that reads: “Workers on strike, unite and fight!” By: Julia Z & Jake S WORCESTER – Students have returned to Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI). Freshmen are being shuttled through new student orientation, professors are dusting off their syllabi, and returning students have long soaked in their remaining days of freedom. Many new students were no doubt won over by WPI’s aggressive promotion of its cutting-edge Robotics Engineering, Computer Science, and AI undergraduate programs along with its highly-celebrated R1 Research University status. Many are surely excited for the “project-based learning” described by eager campus tour guides, ready to sell them a vision of high-tech projects on a charming New England campus. But a university campus is much more than its students, teachers, and overpaid administrators. WPI may claim non-profit status on its tax filings, but in order to compete in a cutthroat higher education industry, it still carries all the fixtures of a corporate enterprise — in many ways, becoming more a landlord/buffet/hedge fund/private police department conglomerate that offers college degrees on the side — including a massive staff force to keep the lights on, the students learning, and the tuition dollars rolling in. So who are the faces that keep those lights on? Who does everything from preparing curriculum, to the research that won WPI its R1 status, to taking out the trash and setting the tables for big donor wine-and-dine sessions? And, more importantly, why are they increasingly becoming self-organized into trade unions to represent them against the interests of WPI’s endowment managers? Working Mass sat down with representatives of three organized labor unions at WPI, plus the campus chapter of the American Association of University Professors (AAUP), to talk about the importance of their work, their organizations, and their conflicts with the bosses on campus. Trades, Groundskeeping, and Custodial Staff Service Employees International Union (SEIU) 32BJ SEIU 32BJ is the international union representing facilities workers at WPI. Without their labor, repairs and maintenance on buildings would go unaddressed, trash would pile up in every classroom and office, and the grass on the Quad wouldn’t get cut — in other words, the campus itself would probably become an overgrown ruin. Every few years, by being organized in their union, facilities staff negotiate a contract with WPI to lay out fair wages, decent benefits, and dignified working conditions. Between every contract cycle, the contract needs to be enforced; the staff, through their union, sometimes find themselves continuing to battle with WPI’s administration to follow the terms of the agreement that both parties have already signed. Mark, a union steward elected by fellow custodians to address such problems on the job, told us about a recent fight, and how the union united his coworkers to push WPI toward a fair resolution that protected their jobs and made their lives easier. About a year ago, the administration brought in consultants from Core America to evaluate the campus practices, supposedly as a checkup to make sure everything was properly staffed and maintained. Core America went to work to cut good union jobs and clamp down on upkeep costs. Part of what they developed was a proposal for communal trash bins in office buildings: rather than entering individual offices to pick up trash and recycling, office staff themselves would take on the work of custodians and deposit their trash in a larger, central bin. Less time spent gathering trash meant WPI could try to get away with paying fewer custodians to do it. The plan would cut five jobs and open the door to more “reorganizations” (i.e., more cuts). As Mark said, nobody thought to talk to custodians themselves about the change. Not only was WPI trying to skip past a contractual obligation to negotiate over these changes with the people who do the work, it wouldn’t even have worked out the way they wanted. “They don’t know anything about our jobs,” Mark said, of the administration and their outside consultants. “If you had office staff doing this, I’d be spending more time getting everything into the right bin than I would have spent just walking through their offices anyway. President Wang used to work at a school that tried this idea out, and that’s exactly what happened.” Union representatives called a meeting with management and were quick to demand the plan be reversed. Union members took collective action by delivering a petition to back up what their reps were saying, and WPI backed down. Core America’s recommendation wouldn’t go through. Mark reflected on the outcome: We got them to open those five positions back up. Did you know they don’t approve purchases in May until the fiscal year ends? At certain points in the year, we have to be really careful with the supplies we have left. Students pay tens of thousands a year to go here, and management has tens of thousands to spend on these consultants, but they want to cut our jobs and make us ration toilet paper? WPI estimates the annual cost of attendance while living on campus — which is required of first- and second-years — to be just shy of $85,000. The total evaluation of its endowment sits at well over half a billion dollars. According to Propublica, in the fiscal year ending June 2025, WPI’s Chief Finance Officer — who reportedly interfaced with Core America consultants — was paid roughly $600,000, while the school’s President took home just over $1 million total. Resident Advisors United Auto Workers (UAW) Local 2322 Resident Advisors (RAs), Residential Mentors (RMs), Community Support Assistants (CSAs), and Community Development Mentors (CDMs) come together to form a union affiliated with United Auto Workers Local 2322. Student workers in any of these four positions perform key roles in keeping students safe, submitting requests for maintenance and repairs, and building community amongst undergraduate students. Without their labor, the dorms would be less safe, less maintained, and much more lonely places to live. We met with Zoey and Dom, two union stewards for this group of workers, which voted to unionize in 2024 and won its first contract with WPI the following year. One core reason the Res Advisor Union (RAU) formed was to challenge constant changes to job descriptions imposed by WPI. In fact, WPI only had a single Res Advisor role, but very soon after RAs won their union election, the administration proposed breaking the job into its current roles, removing most RAs from on-campus housing. Admin claimed this would lighten the workloads of RAs, but Zoey and Dom know it was another cost-cutting measure. Most of the new roles would receive no meal plans, no housing, and less pay. Moreover, RMs would be charged with developing a meaningful relationship with 75 or even 85 students at a time, where in their old role, RAs were only expected to handle around 35. “This seemed to be the personal project of the Dean of Undergraduate Students,” Zoey told us, “but nobody wanted to actually engage with us to figure out a solution that would actually work.” During intense contract negotiations, RAs went on strike from October 31 to December 15, 2025, after which the RAU won a decent contract with WPI that includes just-cause firing, increased pay, housing vouchers, meal plans, and workload caps. And while many of the job description changes were ultimately accepted, they’ll be implemented gradually over a 2 to 3 year phase-in period with a joint Union-Management Committee to oversee the transition. If the new roles aren’t working for Res Advisors themselves, the union will return to the negotiating table in 2028 with an opening to fight again for a better system. Graduate Student Workers United Auto Workers (UAW) Local 2322 Several hundred graduate student workers are organized under the WPI Graduate Workers Union, WPI-GWU, a UAW Local 2322 affiliate. Most doctoral students, and many master’s students, often work as Research Assistants (RAs) or Teaching Assistants (TAs), with others working as administrative staff while pursuing their graduate degree. As a teaching and research institution, the value of this work is obvious. Without TAs, grades wouldn’t be submitted; without RAs, WPI would attract no grant funding; without administrative staffers, very little work could get done at all. Although faculty generally direct teaching and research, graduate workers perform an enormous share of the day-to-day work: office hours; proctoring exams; grading student work; running experiments; and applying for research funds. Stephen is a doctoral student in Biomedical Engineering, a co-chair of WPI-GWU, and an officer in Local 2322, which not only represents grads and res advisors at WPI, but thousands of academic and non-academic workers across New England, including similar workers at UMass Amherst and the University of Vermont. The GWU won its first contract in 2023 after several months of tough negotiations. Prior to the contract, grad workers could barely afford to live in Worcester, and a litany of safety problems plagued their research labs. Stephen told us that some of his colleagues were forced to live on food stamps and simply couldn’t make rent. The ambiguity of their student-worker status even led to delays and complications in receiving worker’s compensation for lab injuries. Their first contract changed everything. Stipend and hourly pay increased as much as 20%; graduate workers were guaranteed paid time off for the first time; WPI now covers the cost of many grad workers’ health insurance, and they now enjoy clear definitions of what’s expected of them at work. Workload caps, just-cause firings, and even new protections and benefits for international students were enshrined in the agreement. Teaching and Research Faculty American Association of University Professors (AAUP) Professor Dan DiMassa is Vice President of WPI’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors (AAUP). At WPI, the AAUP doesn’t function like a traditional labor union, but still represents the organized interests of full- and part-time faculty. Despite the reality of a totally unequal power imbalance between faculty and the university administration that holds hiring and firing authority over them, labor law treats faculty as “managers,” and restricts their rights to organize unions at private institutions like WPI. According to Professor DiMassa, the AAUP chapter at WPI formed in 2018 to deal with the administration’s attempt to rewrite parts of the faculty handbook. Their changes would have undermined academic freedom, putting the right to adjudicate disputes over academic integrity into the hands of trustees and administrators. Since then, the AAUP has also been forced to confront management over COVID-era cuts to faculty retirement benefits, which have only been partially reversed. At WPI, the AAUP chapter often works through the faculty governance system, which is the main mechanism through which faculty can have a say in the development of university policies. Through this channel, despite lacking legal rights to negotiate a union contract, faculty organized under the AAUP have won new tenure-track jobs and enfranchised a new category of teaching faculty. Faculty governance isn’t a perfect way for professors to get what they need, but because they’re organized and can unite in collective action, their conditions stand a chance at improving. Dan told us that the AAUP truly sees the interests of faculty and students as aligned. Both share a common investment in the core educational functions of a university: teaching and research. For the whole system to work, students and faculty alike need to build and maintain an environment of academic freedom where their thoughts can be tested and challenged. Robust faculty governance — capable of struggling against the power of professional university administrators charged with driving up revenue while cutting down on costs — plays an important role in that process. Without its workforce of wage labor, WPI would cease to function, just like any other private enterprise under capitalism. And just like at any other workplace, it’s when workers organize for collective action in their own interests that they can challenge the boss to improve their lives, their workplace, and the world around them. Workers keep the world running, and the working class deserves to run the world! If you want to hear more from Resident Advisors and graduate student workers about their work, their lives, and their labor unions, head to working-mass.com and type “WPI” in the search box! On Wednesday, November 11 at 5:00pm , WPI YDSA — the campus section of Central Mass and Worcester DSA — will facilitate a town hall featuring members of each of the worker organizations we interviewed in this article! Come hear about upcoming contract negotiations of the graduate student workers and facilities staff, and learn more about what it means to be in a union as a part of the working class! Julia Z and Jake S are members of Central Massachusetts & Worcester DSA and contributing writers for Working Mass. The post Stiffing Workers, Rationing Toilet Paper: Who Really Makes WPI Run? appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: Six Hail Marys: Thoughts of an ICU RN
articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content: By Asanti M. The conversation surrounding healthcare access is more than an abstraction of cost and risk, it’s life and death, and people are dying. I know because I’ve pronounced them. I know because I’ve cleaned their lifeless bodies. The burdens of the ailing are only compounded by the general disservice of our institutional frameworks. The nebulous jargon tossed around boardrooms and between pundits materializes in the financial reality that confronts the humanity of the unfortunate and the ailing. I’ve seen eyes full of pain, the walls of life crumbling around them, forced to discuss the finances of death, because let me be clear, dying is a very expensive endeavor hear in the States, and God forbid you attempt to hold on to life! The junction of societal divides is never so transparent as the time spent dying in Intensive Care. How perverse a world we’ve been forced into when the sick and dying are seen as another avenue for profit. When the burden of ailment and disease ceases to be a collective human struggle and becomes the burden of one. Oh what a beautiful freedom we have here in the States to accumulate our wealth from wherever we please, the opportunities are endless; no rite, no life stands too sacred as to not fall at the altar of Capital. Oh what freedom we’re blessed with! Blessed are those whose conscious is freed from the suffering of their brothers and sisters; blessed are those whose life is freed from the collective struggle against ailment. There’s a pity as lifeless as my patients, offered to those unfortunate enough to be poor. As if their lack of wealth taints their souls and damns them not in the next life, but right here in this one. How many hours should they have to work to pay off the death of their father, of their daughter, of their son? Fret not, those numbers are meticulously calculated by the profiteers who mandate we exist in such a carnivorous system. We’re told by those with the wealth of a small nation that there’s no money to alleviate this collective suffering within the bounds of the current structure. If that’s truly the case, then it’s time we rid ourselves of the current structure. Any system that allows for such obscene levels of wealth to congeal into individual hands while the multitude counts pennies on their death beds must go. What principle do you cling to, to justify the needless death and stress of the sick? What sort of perverse freedom precludes the Preservation of Life! Blessed are the stars and stripes! If only the poor had sacrificed more to accumulate Capital, maybe their death wouldn’t be so distasteful; maybe their death wouldn’t be burdened by bills, and they could focus on their grief. What a sordid freedom the nation takes pride in. Our government cries, “how much”, “at what cost”, as they calculate the expense of expanding Healthcare. Look in this bed, there lies your cost! There, lifeless and grey! Can the nation not see the cost! Is it the grey? Maybe if we cast them green and stamped “e pluribus unum” on their forehead they would see. What a beautiful freedom we have here. Six Hail Marys, Lord let it be known that my brother has died at the altar of Capital in the sordid name of our perverse Freedom! The post Six Hail Marys: Thoughts of an ICU RN first appeared on Red Fault .

articles.title: Socialists Can Never Win — Until We Do
articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content: By Nolan R. This article was originally published in Democratic Left: Find it here We all know the narrative by now: socialists are too radical, fringe, and unpopular to win any kind of lasting power. “Enjoy your time in the sun, lefties, because any moment now the hammer of reasonable, moderate thought will come crashing down and send you back to the depths of political obscurity with your collective tail tucked between your legs.” Variations of this line are repeated constantly across the country by national media and prominent members of both parties. They repeat it like a mantra, both because they need it to be true and because they would rather eat glass than honestly engage with our ideas. Unfortunately for them, the recent streak of socialist victories has proven there is immense hunger for a working-class movement in this country. In fact, DSA may be more popular among Democratic voters than the Democratic Party itself . One out of three Democratic voters now identify as democratic socialists , and even among those who don’t, two-thirds would be comfortable voting for one. How does the media react when a socialist wins against allegedly insurmountable odds? They minimize. They put Zohran’s victory down to personality and social media presence , not policy. When a slate of DSA candidates won across multiple levels of government, they said that’s just New York . When DSA won in Denver , Philadelphia , Washington DC , and Detroit , well, those are all reliably blue areas, so what’s the big deal? On the other hand, they pounce on any whiff of failure as an opportunity to discredit the entire movement. Fox News triumphantly declared Kai Newkirk’s loss in Arizona a “setback” for DSA even though Newkirk only became a member days before requesting an endorsement , and was not endorsed in his primary. Similarly, they label progressive politicians like Abdul El-Sayed “commies in camouflage” despite his self-identification as a “capitalist who believes in regulation.” Their goal is to erase nuance, lumping anyone to the left of Stephen Miller into the same communist boogeyman so they can tar us all with the same brush. Francesca Hong started her campaign for governor of Wisconsin as a little-known state assembly member going up against the full weight of the Democratic establishment and still managed to come within a razor-thin margin of the nomination as an open socialist in a swing state. Outspent by several orders of magnitude, she relied on a robust canvassing operation of enthusiastic volunteers. Her narrow loss proves the viability of insurgent socialist campaigns even in states conventionally considered moderate. To the New York Times , however, the results represent a brick wall for DSA’s momentum . It would be much more sensible, pundits and political operatives argue, to nominate safe, unchallenging centrists who promise nothing and deliver less. Otherwise, we might spook the independent voters, sink the Democrats in the upcoming midterms , and doom us all to a freshly empowered Trump administration. The goal is to browbeat the voting public into believing that holding principled positions opens the door to fascism. If Democrats stand for nothing, then there’s nothing for Republicans to criticize, right? This narrative is bullshit. It assumes that independent voters’ politics lie smack dab between Republicans and Democrats, but the reality isn’t so simple. While most independents describe themselves as moderate , they also tend to hold an assortment of incongruent beliefs, such as support for universal healthcare . Rather than diehard centrists, they often refuse to identify with power (hence the independent label) and feel abandoned by both parties. Corporate media endlessly promote pundits who complain that Democrats have gone too far left instead of admitting that many voters are disillusioned by the cycle of optimism and disappointment that comes with electing milquetoast Democrats. Millions of Americans voted for Obama or Biden with the earnest belief that they would get the change they were hoping for and then they were duped into supporting a vessel for the capitalist status quo . Despite the hand-wringing, independents and the politically disaffected are fertile ground for DSA’s growing constituency. Each DSA win forces the mainstream media to move the goalposts and adjust their narrative. They argued that AOC and Zohran were outliers, that we could only win in New York City, that we couldn’t win in swing states like Michigan. Now, they’re arguing that we can’t win in competitive races against Republicans. How will the narrative shift again when we prove them wrong? In all likelihood, they’ll double down on the idea that DSA’s success will hurt Democrats in the midterms. After the midterms, they’ll likely argue that while socialism may be gaining in popularity, our policies will inevitably fail. No electoral success will prod the hostile media into fairly appraising our program or our candidates. At the end of the day, we shouldn’t internalize the bad-faith criticisms of the corporate media and the party duopoly. The fact that the media can’t stop talking about us, that they’re so obviously terrified of an ascendant Left , means that we are on the right track. We will harness this energy and attention that’s being focused on us, and we will ride that wave to victory. We are now the largest socialist organization in the history of the United States, with 120,000 members and counting. Our names and our ideas are echoing in hushed tones throughout the halls of power. The president and the speaker of the house describe our movement in apocalyptic terms while the Senate holds McCarthyist show trials alleging connections to terror . While they lie about our goals and our methods, they are right to be afraid. We threaten to seize the reins of power that the ruling class has taken for granted for so long and to deliver them into the hands of the people. More than ever, it seems that a better world is possible. Keep winning, DSA. The post Socialists Can Never Win — Until We Do first appeared on Red Fault .

articles.title: Texas Wasn’t Always a Right-Wing Evangelical Powerhouse
articles.author: David Griscom
articles.content: There’s a common view of religious history that holds that the further back you go, the stronger the smell of brimstone and the more conservative the beliefs. It isn’t true, and it obscures how much the human hand makes the world, including our ideas of the sacred. Joseph L. Locke’s new book One State Under God: A History of Religion in Texas is an important reminder that the conservative evangelical Christianity that dominates Texas, and through it has consolidated its influence over the country, was not a natural outgrowth of Christianity itself, but a product of historical developments. Texas today is at the forefront of the campaign to tear down the wall between church and state. The Bible has been reintroduced in Texas classrooms, along with a new law requiring classrooms to display the protestant version of the Ten Commandments. Texas gave the country the prosperity gospel preached by televangelists, including the megachurch pastor and multimillionaire Joel Osteen. The state has been the proving ground for a fiery marriage between evangelicalism and conservatism. Religion has been woven through Texas history, and in turn Texas has woven a particular form of religion into American life. But in One State Under God , Locke shows that the marriage of Texas conservatism and evangelicalism was never preordained. Indeed, Texas was once considered a “godless” land. Christianity did not come easily to Texas. The first imperial attempt to impose it failed. Spain saw Texas as a bulwark against French expansion but never conquered it, physically or religiously. The missions of San Antonio, ancient by American standards, were sparsely populated. When Mexico declared independence from Spain, only two priests remained in Texas — and neither, observed the Tejano revolutionary Juan Seguín, was particularly religious. A Spanish official lamented the failure to make Texas a Catholic land, writing that it remained “under the domination of the barbarian.” Locke takes us through Mexican and revolutionary Texas, where religious expansion ran into similar obstacles. For most of this period, the governance of Texas was an afterthought — the territory was administered as part of Coahuila y Tejas, literally tacked onto a neighboring Mexican state. And religion was an afterthought, too. There was scant religious infrastructure in early Texas. Most of the Anglo migrants were protestants of the frontier variety, whose faith ran on circuit riders and camp meetings rather than settled clergy and church buildings, and Mexico had little interest in supplying Texas with priests. Much of life was secular: children went unbaptized, marriages went unrecognized, and burials were conducted in secular graveyards. Texans today may be taken for a religious bunch, but in those years they were seen as living at the edge of civilization, godless and rough. As a Presbyterian minister wrote at the time, these Texans “generally appear in their personal depravity to have forgot if ever they did know or pretend to believe, that there was a God, or a devil,” and behaved as though “as soon as they had crossed the Sabine line, they considered also that they had passed over the line of spiritual accountability.” When conservative politicians call on Texas to embrace its Christian roots, then, it’s not entirely clear what roots they’re talking about. The Bible Belt Gets Its Buckle Anyone who has spent time in the South today can see the sway that Christianity holds over our politics. It wasn’t always so. According to Locke, a term like “Bible Belt” would have drawn puzzled looks in the early twentieth century. Nationally, “the South was not yet seen as an especially religious region, and religion did not seem particularly active in public life there.” Most religious Texans considered this a good thing. Separation of church and state was taken seriously by Texas politicians and Texas Baptists alike, who believed that it kept religion “pure and left the rest of the world to its hellish ways.” What, then, brought Texas evangelicals into politics? One State Under God supplies the answer: prohibition, the jingoism of World War I, and the Ku Klux Klan. The fight over alcohol was the opening salvo. Governor Oscar Colquitt defeated his prohibitionist challengers in 1910 by stoking the state’s long-standing opposition to religious rule, saying, “The place of a preacher is in the pulpit and not in politics.” But his victory was short-lived, as the forces that had amassed to outlaw drinking on religious grounds found they rather enjoyed politics as a means of social purification. By the early 1920s, the prohibitionists had won, the war had made loyalty a religious test, and the Klan had put a hundred thousand Texans in white robes. The preacher who best understood what all of that made possible was J. Frank Norris, who can be thought of as the nation’s first megachurch leader. Norris preached a fiery, reactionary Christianity, condemning communists, liberals, modernists, Catholics, and Jews. He turned on Baylor University, his own alma mater and the world’s largest Baptist college, hounding a professor out of his job for teaching evolution. He made common cause with the Klan. And he had a violent streak: Norris was tried for arson in 1912, and in 1926 he shot an unarmed man dead in his church office. He was acquitted both times. Starting with a congregation of little more than a dozen, Norris built a church of thousands, and his radio show and newspaper reached many more. He founded a second church in Detroit and spent the 1930s flying back and forth between the two, in the early days of aviation. Norris had influence, and he used it. When the Democrats nominated Al Smith for president in 1928, Norris raged against the Catholic from New York, prophesying that if a Catholic won power, “they would behead every Protestant preacher and disembowel every Protestant mother. They would burn to ashes every Protestant Church and dynamite every Protestant school.” Conspiratorial and paranoid religiosity had been let loose in Texas politics, and it would stay. God and Landlords The rise of conservative evangelical Christianity happened against the backdrop of two major mobilizations of working-class Texans. The first was the populist uprising, which united laborers and farmers, white and black, in a People’s Party that vied for power with the ruling Democrats. That movement was put down violently , and the defeat was followed by severe restrictions on the vote — not only for black Texans but for poor whites as well. Then the Socialist Party of Texas competed with the Democrats for the support of tenant farmers across the state. When James Edward “Pa” Ferguson won the governor’s mansion, he did it largely on a platform of tenant-farmer reforms lifted from the Socialist Party. Both movements leaned heavily on religion. Locke notes that Christianity shaped the populists, and that the movement borrowed organizational methods from the Methodists, like sending out traveling lecturers. As I observed in my own book on Texas’s populist past, Thomas Lewis Nugent, one of the movement’s major leaders and its candidate for governor, called the life of Jesus Christ the “beginning of Christian socialism.” Black populist leaders like John B. Rayner preached to rural Texans as well. But Locke argues that despite these more radical strains, “Texas’s new wealth infected the Baptists and the Methodists and the Presbyterians,” especially once the oil boom erupted. His account of the two Christianities that divided Texas through slavery and Reconstruction is the book at its strongest: one belonging to the slaveholders, which preached a paternalistic apologetics for chattel slavery, and one belonging to black Texans, which held out liberation for the enslaved and judgment for the wicked in the next life. It is a distinction he largely stops drawing once emancipation arrives — a shame, because the decades that follow are full of it. Take the example of John B. Rayner. After the defeat of the populist uprising, he began taking money from the same landlords and bosses he had once opposed and wound up in the employ of the lumber baron John Henry Kirby, no longer speaking of liberation or the cooperative commonwealth but of personal responsibility and the self-help programs of Booker T. Washington. Kirby at the time was trying to break the Brotherhood of Timber Workers, one of the first interracial unions in the South. What Rayner was hired to do, preachers were hired to do across the cotton fields of Texas and the South: attack the “sinful ways” of the poor and keep their attention off the men robbing them. This was a Christianity bankrolled by the wealthy to keep working people in line. Locke does not ignore the alliance between the evangelical movement and the rich; he shows in detail how religion in Texas was cultivated for political ends. What he leaves out is this particular use of it, as a weapon against the agrarian revolts of the populists and then the socialists, who had made religion a common language for uniting tenant farmers across the state. Texas is a big place with a long history, and any book about it has to make cuts. In the decades that followed, the familiar alliance between evangelical Christianity and free-market conservatism came into the open. As Locke notes, the change was captured in Ronald Reagan’s line to a gathering of evangelical leaders in Dallas in 1980: “I know that you can’t endorse me, but I want you to know that I endorse you.” That rally was organized by the Texas televangelist James Robison, and men like him had by then steamrolled what was left of the prohibitions on religion in politics. The long campaign to remake religion in the image of the Right was complete. Today Texans live in the evangelical right’s world: abortion is banned, the Ten Commandments hang in classrooms, and the Texas GOP has its eyes on ending no-fault divorce. But the great service of One State Under God is to show that this world was deliberately made — and that what was made can be unmade.
